#882. Alonso crisis deepens as chaotic Chelsea lose and fans taunt own player

It always feels like Chelsea are not far away from a crisis and Xabi Alonso has now lost more Premier League games this season than Manchester United.

Alonso will inevitably come under further scrutiny after another alarming result and performance, with unpopular centre-back Wesley Fofana also targeted by Chelsea’s supporters.

Chants of “f--- off Fofana, you’re not wanted here” were clearly heard from the away end after another excruciating experience for the defender.

After an ill-advised interview earlier this week, Fofana followed that up with a string of mistakes which led to Nottingham Forest’s second goal.

Forest have secured 11 of their 12 points against clubs in the perceived “Big Six” and Aston Villa, who are competing in the Champions League, and did not deserve the scoreline to be as close.

Alonso is the latest Chelsea manager to become embroiled in chaos before Christmas and four defeats from five league matches will not make happy reading for the hierarchy.

His defence appear to be nervous wrecks and in his desperation to toughen them up he opted to play Moisés Caicedo in what was a peculiar line-up.

Chelsea have conceded 23 goals in the league and until they improve that record, Alonso will find it impossible to retain the club’s backing.

“Everyone in the club needs to stick together and we have to deal with it,” he said. “We are going through a difficult moment with solidity and confidence, we need to find solutions.

“Everyone in the team is needed and I am thinking about the next games and we will see [if Fofana is picked for the next game]. We need to support everyone and if we don’t, things will get more complicated.”

Forest responded after their insipid performance at Bournemouth last weekend to secure another notable home result for Oliver Glasner.

He must be hoping that Forest’s owner, Evangelos Marinakis, turns up for every game.

Marinakis was in attendance for only the second time this season and, on his last visit, witnessed a stirring victory over Manchester City.

Morgan Gibbs-White scored twice to win the private battle of the England No 10s, with Chelsea’s Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers both ineffective.

Glasner said: “We feel we are heading in the right direction but there is still a lot to do. Twelve points from 12 games is still not satisfying for us, but wins like this help us show the players that it is working.

“If you have back-to-back wins against City and Chelsea you must be doing many things really well.”

Xaver Schlager provides a beautiful assist for Morgan Gibbs-White to restore Nottingham Forest's two-goal lead 🎯 https://t.co/zpkElGvNJy

While Glasner is seeing clear signs of progress, the problems are piling up for Alonso.

Chelsea are never far away from a crisis and this feels like a big night for Xabi Alonso.

Three defeats in the last four Premier League games, including a thrashing by Leeds in their last match, has cranked up the pressure.

This was always likely to be a long-term project, however, and Chelsea remain convinced Alonso will lead them into a bright new era.

Until then, there are going to be some tricky times ahead. Chelsea are as wildly unpredictable as the team they face this evening at the City Ground.

They would leapfrog Coventry regardless of the margin of victory, as they already have a better goal difference.

A draw would see them remain 17th, while a really heavy defeat might see them fall to 18th.

Glasner conceded, in his own press conference, that he had hoped for better results so far this season.

He said: “We wanted and expected more to be honest, but it is still early. We look at what we need to improve and work on it. I’m no magician, I have no dust I can spread at the training ground.

“From my experience, everything is hard work and we need to improve our individual mistakes and defence. We need to improve our efficiency in attack and set pieces. We still haven’t scored from a set piece.”

He added that the club wanted a good atmosphere for the evening kick-off, saying that, “is what we want and need. Friday night under the flood lights - it’s crucial. Our fans want a great weekend.”

Earlier in the week, Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana said he could now “laugh” about a recent penalty miss against Liverpool in the Carabao Cup.

While the statement went down badly amongst some supporters, Fofana has apologised, and Alonso told a pre-match press conference he was ready to move on.

He told journalists: “Absolutely, we have addressed that with him and for sure it was unfortunate.

“He apologised, he knows it was not right the moment, it was not right the content, we are here to take things seriously and he said that it’s not going to be repeated and we know that it’s something that we don’t want, these kind of things, and they are not going to be repeated for sure.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Nottingham Forest vs Chelsea.

The City Ground hosts the Premier League clash tonight, with two sides who are both falling short of expectations.

Forest head coach Oliver Glasner brought with him a sense of optimism after he left Crystal Palace, but the club are just outside the bottom three, sitting in 17th position with only nine points. As things stand, they are only clear of 18th-placed Sunderland because of superior goal difference.

Beneath them, Glasner’s former club Palace are bottom, two points away from them, and then Manchester United come in 19th, a single point behind. With Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino now installed at Selhurst Park and Old Trafford, respectively, the pressure could soon be felt yet more keenly.

There have been flashes of encouragement, with a 3-1 win over Manchester City in early November, spearheaded by a brace from Liam Delap, who left Chelsea in the summer. However, last Saturday they lost 2-0 at Bournemouth to dent any nascent momentum, and the match was the sixth in 11 league games where the club have failed to score. Forest have scored nine times this season, with only Sunderland having a worse record in attack.

Chelsea’s Xabi Alonso has also endured a tough time of late. They were trounced 4-1 against Leeds United at home on Saturday, despite taking the lead in the first half.

That worrying collapse was the fourth loss in five league matches, and it followed a 1-0 defeat against Sunderland at the Stadium of Light before the recent international break.

There is speculation that Chelsea will move for a central defender in January, with 20 goals conceded in the Premier League so far.

Chelsea are currently in eighth place in the league with 16 points, five points behind Liverpool in fourth. Tonight, they could leapfrog Bournemouth, who are in fifth, two points ahead of them. Another loss, though, could see them in the bottom half once the weekend’s fixtures are completed.

#881. Ten-man Bournemouth battle back to score Europa League victory at Celta Vigo

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Celta Vigo 1-2 Bournemouth: The Cherries lost Bafode Diakite to a 23rd-minute red card but battled back from going a goal behind to win in Spain

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Bournemouth moved a step closer to automatic qualification for the Europa League last 16 after coming from behind with 10 men to win 2-1 at Celta Vigo.

It was a remarkable 10th victory in a row in all competitions for Marco Rose’s side and it might have been the most satisfying of the lot for the manager, coming as it did after his team had found themselves a goal down and a man down at half-time.

The visitors looked in trouble when, minutes after Iago Aspas had curled Celta in front, Bafode Diakite was red-carded for a poorly timed tackle.

Bournemouth might have folded then, but instead they came roaring back, Alvaro Rodriguez heading them level almost immediately after the start of the second half.

A draw would have been an excellent result in the circumstances. Substitute Rayan had other ideas, waiting at the end of a rapid breakaway to sweep in the winner 12 minutes from time.

Victory against Viktoria Plzen in December will almost certainly now be enough to earn direct passage to the last 16.

Pablo Duran had the ball in the Bournemouth net after 10 minutes after it spilled back to him off Michele Di Gregorio, the goalkeeper relieved to see the offside flag go up against the Celta striker.

The stand-in keeper redeemed himself minutes later with a solid save from an outrageous bicycle kick by Aspas. It would have been a remarkable goal but the Celta great would not be denied. Bournemouth failed fully to get the ball away, and from the edge of the box Aspas curled a beauty in off the far post.

Bournemouth had gone behind in the first half of their last game in this competition at Sparta Prague. That night, the balance was tipped almost immediately in their favour by a red card for the Czech side, but here it was Rose’s team who found themselves down to 10 men.

Diakite made an honest attempt to win the ball but was late and his studs landed on the ankle of Couhaib Driouech. An initial yellow card was overturned following a VAR check and Bournemouth were on the ropes.

It had been the most challenging half of their debut European campaign, but within minutes of the start of the second period, they were level.

Amine Adli was left in space outside the box to send over a wonderful cross to the far post. Arriving there was Rodriguez, sneaking ahead of his defender to get a head on the ball and nod in the equaliser.

A wonderful counter-attack brought the Premier League side their winner. Adrien Truffert showed good strength out on left to outmuscle Sergio Carreira, and he fed the ball up to Marcus Tavernier. He might have shot himself but instead moved it on to Rayan who swept home.

#880. Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.

"Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he said on Sunday.

But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.

"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp said ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.

"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement."

If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his plan to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.

That plan, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.

It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a new FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.

Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.

Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president" in October.

Those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and said that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.

Proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.

The 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.

"I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world."

But the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (CAF) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.

In fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".

But, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be announced on Tuesday.

While Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

#879. Thomas Frank ‘close to a heart attack’ in dramatic first Crystal Palace win

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Jean-Philippe Mateta and Dwight McNeil scored late in a 2-1 Europa League victory over Real Sociedad

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thomas Frank secured his first win as Crystal Palace boss but admitted his new side nearly nearly gave him a “heart attack” in the nervy final five minutes of their 2-1 Europa League comeback against 10-man Real Sociedad.

Chelsea loanee Mamadou Sarr broke the deadlock for the visitors in the 66th minute at Selhurst Park but Frank’s first home contest turned on its head when Jon Martin received a second yellow card six minutes later.

Jean-Philippe Mateta drew the sides level from the penalty spot and Dwight McNeil poked Palace into the lead from fellow substitute Jorgen Strand Larsen’s bicycle kick, but they were denied a chance to put the game away when Yeremy Pino’s penalty was saved.

“I think first and foremost to get it over the line, and (it was) an extremely important win for various reasons,” said Frank, who took charge of Premier League basement club Palace for the first time in Saturday’s league loss to Coventry.

“One, of course, confidence, and it relates to belief against an extremely good team. I think the first half we were compact and very disciplined in many ways. We missed the high-pressure situations we had, and I think we struggled to keep the ball well enough.

“Second half I felt we were much better in the high pressure, and I felt we kept the ball much better. I actually felt we got a bit more momentum in the second half but then, out of the blue, they scored the 1-0 goal.

“But what I really like is the belief from the players, what they showed, and that we are threatening on set-pieces, we cannot underestimate that.”

Unai Marrero’s save to deny Pino from the spot kept the Spanish side in with a chance of an equaliser and it nearly came at the death from Orri Oskarsson, whose effort was pushed away by Dean Henderson – his last of six saves on Thursday night.

“We know in football one moment can change the game,” Frank continued. “The penalty and the red card changed the game, then we still needed to score.

“To win still is important and we went brave, we went with the offensive substitutions and kept two strikers on the pitch, and that paid off.

“And then I think we were all close to getting a heart attack in the last five minutes.”

Frank agreed the win could be a significant turning point for Palace’s fortunes ahead of a critical Premier League clash with Hull on Sunday.

“That’s why it’s so important to keep doing the right things, keep believing, and keep going,” he said.

Palace’s Premier League survival remains the priority but the result also propelled the Eagles into play-off position in their European campaign, four places out of the top eight after five matches.

Asked about his ambitions for the European campaign – given Palace’s league position – Frank replied: “I think we want to aim high.

“We are ambitious for this tournament, and that’s why the win was so important.”

#878. 'Priceless' Duran proves 'the man' but is he papering over cracks at Celtic?

Camilo Duran's 15-goal haul this season has made him an invaluable player for a Celtic side fighting for European progression

"Duran is priceless for us at the moment".

It would be difficult for a football manager to muster up a higher compliment for one of his players - given he should know exactly how much he did cost - but Celtic boss Martin O'Neill was rightly effusive in his praise for Camilo Duran.

With 15 goals in 23 appearances, six assists, and another late European winner on Thursday, the Colombian was once again the main man for a struggling Celtic side.

His double against Besiktas breathed life into their Europa League campaign last time out, and his late leap to nod in the winner against Torreense kept it alive.

Duran, 24, started on the bench but was brought on with just over half an hour to go as O'Neill watched his side labour against a team currently 13th in the Portuguese second tier.

Celtic would still be searching for their first European win were it not for their summer arrival from Qarabag, whose goals have played a key part in keeping his team within touching distance of a play-off spot with three fixtures to play.

"He's taken on this mantle of being the man and he's been fantastic," said O'Neill, who started Duran on the bench. "We tried a similar approach against Besiktas.

"Sometimes by the time Duran gets subbed on, you could be behind. But I think that's the sign of a brilliant player, he'll do something.

"He's not a big guy but he's just a super footballer, a super, super footballer."

'He's priceless for us' - O'Neill on match winner Duran

Duran's summer arrival was overshadowed when, just over a fortnight later, a club-record fee was paid to Bodo Glimt for another striker, Kasper Hogh.

While recent weeks have been dominated by debates over Duran or Hogh, the debate now seems settled, with the Colombian operating on a different level from his striking counterpart.

Anyone watching Celtic in Portugal would have watched Hogh find space a handful of times in the area, but repeatedly fail to find a team-mate or trouble the goalkeeper. Duran didn't need to be asked twice.

"I don't know how many touches he got, but he had the telling touch," James McFadden said on Sportsound post-match.

Duran's goals have also proved decisive in securing domestic points against Falkirk and Hibernian, and with Celtic just a point clear of Rangers, he is indeed invaluable.

Despite his late header giving the thousands of travelling Celtic fans a thrilling end to a relatively turgid game, the intervention is another significant moment in a season that is threatening to unravel if individual performances fail to continue papering over glaring deficiencies across the park.

If the lively Jota - who lasted 74 minutes - was not creating chances, tormenting full-backs or digging out enticing crosses in the first half, Celtic seemed without any real plan of attack.

Yang and Luke McCowan's involvements were limited at best, Hogh's chance to stake a claim was sub-par to be kind, and there was no driving force from the middle of the park to show some impetus.

Arithmetically, Celtic can still finish in any position in the Europa League table. But if they are to claim a playoff or automatic qualification spot, they will need Duran to remain in such a rich vein of form.

Duran spares Celtic's blushes against Portuguese second-tier side Torreense

Celtic news, views and analysis all in one place

Brian: Embarrassed by that performance, I know that there no easy games in Europe, couldn't pass the ball, not fit enough, no style of play and poorly coached. The club is in decline.

John: Celtic are just an average side these days - there should be no expectation.

Ted: That was just embarrassing. The 31st team in Portugal made us look ordinary. Go now Martin with dignity intact and preserve your achievements. Thus mob will drag you down.

Allan: Outclassed and out paced by Torreense, Celtic played poorly with a lot of comedy of errors in their play. But Yippee hee, Celtic. Won with a late goal from Duran.

Liam: This can't go on any further now, regardless of the result. MON is done and the coaching staff are done. Booing substitutions is the end, never mind a performance like this against second division opposition. The board can resign too.

Alec: Total embarrassment. Barring Jota, there was a complete lack of creativity, quality, urgency and belief. Time for the board to make the right decisions, get a new manager in and get rid of at least 10 of those players on show tonight.

#877. Levski Sofia fans hospitalised after violent clashes with Marseille supporters

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Bulgarian Football Union has referred the incident to Uefa

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Marseille head coach Bruno Genesio said “we are living through violent times” after five Levski Sofia fans were hospitalised following violent clashes before their Europa League encounter with the French side.

Groups of supporters threw projectiles and flares and French outlet L’Equipe reported that there were Nazi salutes observed in the away section.

Ten minutes before kick-off at the Stade Velodrome a group of Marseille fans broke through into the away stand, which housed around 500 fans.

In the ensuing clashes five people, all Bulgarian, were injured and taken to hospital “with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder”, according to the Marseille police prefecture, while six others were treated on-site for more superficial injuries.

The police force said there was “no information at this stage regarding any arrests”.

Security were able to restore order and the game kicked off on time, although there were further incidents later on, particularly at half-time.

Genesio said: “We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable.” Julio Velazquez, head coach of the Bulgarian domestic champions, said: “It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football.”

The Bulgarian Football Union condemned the violence and said it had referred the incident to UEFA, calling for the harshest possible sanctions. It also demanded full cooperation and transparency from French authorities in investigating the attacks and identifying those responsible.

Levski said the club's priority is the safety and well-being of its fans. A statement read: “What happened tonight is particularly alarming given the extraordinary security measures put in place by the French authorities, as well as the restrictions imposed on our travelling supporters—restrictions that the club had already formally contested with UEFA.

“Despite the risks identified by the club prior to the match, the measures taken failed to provide adequate protection for our fans. This is completely unacceptable.”

Marseille also condemned the violence and said it is conducting “a thorough analysis of the circumstances in which these incidents took place.”

Bulgarian President Iliana Yotova called for those responsible to be held accountable and Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he had spoken to French president Emmanuel Macron about the violence at a European summit in Brussels.

A spokesperson for Macron’s office said: “He condemned in the strongest possible terms these acts of violence targeting Bulgarian supporters, which have no place in sport or in public spaces, and assured the Prime Minister that these acts would not go unpunished.”

Marseille won the game 1-0, with Amine Gouiri scoring a 28th-minute penalty.

#876. COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels

The preliminary agreement at UN climate talks in Turkey calls for a rapid reduction of planet-warming emissions and at least $120 billion to help countries adapt to climate change.

COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).

The goal of other co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text. The draft emphasizes clean energy but notes that "electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix" — an approach that has proved divisive at the talks, with many insisting that electrification be strictly tied to renewable energy.

Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is important because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.

"The new negotiating text contains all the necessary building blocks for a successful outcome to the conference: from the goal of climate neutrality for all industrialized countries by 2030 to a work program that can keep the 1.5-degree limit in place," said Greenpeace Germany head Martin Kaiser on Monday.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The draft expressed "deep concern" that the 1.5 Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) temperature threshold agreed at the 2015 COP in Paris to avoid runaway climate change was now out of reach. It stressed the need for "accelerating action to minimize both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and to return global warming to below 1.5C as soon as possible."

Recognizing a need to address rising carbon emissions, the draft highlighted efforts to "urgently and rapidly" scale up controversial technologies to capture and store CO2 to bring down atmospheric carbon levels.

"For the first time, all the parties here are grappling with the fact that the world will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees. Negotiators must deliver a response," said Ani Dasgupta, president of the World Resources Institute, adding that this meant going beyond slashing emissions.

"This requires scaling carbon removal through both nature-based solutions like restoring forests and wetlands, or emerging technologies that directly capture carbon from air," he told reporters.

Kaiser, however, criticized the lack of binding commitments in the draft's resolutions. He added that Europe should work with China and the most climate-vulnerable countries to keep oil-producing nations, including Russia and countries in the Middle East, from "undermining the conference's decisions and turning them into a free pass for the oil and gas industry."

Other activists have dismissed carbon capture as a "false solution" being promoted by corporations.

Cosima Cassel, an expert at climate think tank E3G, was cautiously pleased with the draft's "ambitious language" but said it appeared the broad deal would now leave negotiators to "fight for trade-offs."

"The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defense of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance," she said in a statement.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Disagreements over financing largely relate to who should bear the costs of international climate action, whether financial support should be provided through grants or loans, and how funding for developing countries can be increased.

Representatives of developing nations and small island states, regions bearing the brunt of the climate crisis, have protested climate inaction and a lack of financial support in recent days.

"Climate finance isn't an extra at these talks: it's the condition for everything else," said Rukiya Khamis, program manager for East Africa with environmental group 350.org. "It's alarming how financial pledges by wealthy, polluting countries are dropping like a stone — COP31 must stop this with a strong outcome on adaptation finance."

"Now we must fight to keep this [adaption finance] in the final decision and ensure these promises become real, grant-based money," said Harjeet Singh of the Fill The Fund campaign, which calls on rich countries and corporations to deliver the funding needed for climate-related loss and damage, such as homes destroyed by floods and harvests ruined by drought.

"Communities are suffering devastating losses and damages today precisely because we failed to deliver adaptation at the right time," added Singh.

At 18 pages and 144 items, the draft will be the focus of lengthy discussions in the coming days as delegates try to come to an agreement by Friday. Some observers went so far as to say the document's scope was too wide to be taken seriously.

"The draft final declaration reads like a Christmas wish list," said Niklas Höhne, a climate policy expert at the NewClimate Institute in Germany. "There are even several points on which we will obviously not be able to reach a consensus, including for example the proposal that developed countries achieve net-zero emissions by 2030."

But Chris Bowen, chief of negotiations and Australia's minister for climate change and energy, appeared optimistic.

"The general tenor and tone [of the talks] has been very constructive," he told reporters Monday. "Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you'd expect […] [but] they've also come in the spirit of cooperation, the spirit of respect and a spirit where parties have said to me that they want to help get an outcome."

David Waskow, director of WRI's International Climate Initiative, said the draft text showed a level of "seriousness" on important issues like finance, electrification, oceans, overshoot scenarios and emissions of greenhouse gases including methane, which has a warming impact more than 80 times stronger than CO2.

"The question is whether the level of ambition on those issues is carried through into the final outcome here," said Waskow. "And that's what we need to be watching closely over the coming days."

Additional reporting by Tim Schauenberg in Antalya.

Update, November 17, 2026: This article has been updated with additional reactions to the draft text.

#875. What makes or breaks a high press?

Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz spearhead Liverpool's press under Andoni Iraola

A good high press has been the basis for some of the most successful sides in modern football but a well-oiled pressing machine has many moving parts - all requiring close attention.

When an out-of-possession plan is implemented poorly, entire seasons can fall apart.

So, what determines whether a press works or fails? And how are the always-adapting Premier League teams exploiting high presses this season?

When a team decides to press, they must first establish their intention. This informs how the players act.

Speaking to DAZN Portugal, Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler was asked about whether a good press relied more on physicality or courage.

"When you want to press high you need the courage and mindset to do it. Our mindset is we press to score, we don't just press to win the ball back."

In coaching, clarity is key - particularly when it comes to creating alignment in the squad and Hurzeler is deliberate in simplifying big ideas when delivering messages to his players, a skill he practised as a radio pundit during the World Cup.

"[Punditry] helps you as a coach in that you have to summarise things in a short and easy way so that everyone understands," he said. "Football might get more complex but simplicity counts."

Hurzeler's "pressing to score" is a phrase that communicates many ideas in a memorable three words: intensity, being proactive, and immediate forward-thinking on winning the ball.

It also frames pressing in a way that makes it easy for attackers to buy into, in the form of goals.

"You want commitment from everyone on the pitch," Hurzeler explained.

"If just one has doubts, the whole press is gone."

The Red Bull school of coaching uses a similarly succinct phrase - "the last step" to address these ideas around intention, collectiveness and aggression.

Summarised by Tactx, whose coaches have worked under the Red Bull model, the last step refers to "players [being] coached to attack through the opponent, using the final step to lunge aggressively at the ball".

"This action commits the defender fully and is often the decisive moment that allows possession to be won."

Pressing to engage rather than just to close distances ensures the team in possession aren't given the time or space to play through otherwise half-hearted pressure.

Applying team-wide pressure, Newcastle make a strong tackle and win the ball.

This forces a turnover that puts Newcastle in a favourable attacking position.

When discussing how good or bad a team is at pressing, how much they run is often brought up. But the distance a team covers fails to paint the full picture when it comes to the effectiveness of a team's pressing strategy.

Liverpool's current boss Andoni Iraola was asked about how he interpreted physical data last year.

"It's not 'we run a lot, so we are good,' no," he said. "The high-speed running, the sprint speeds [matter for us] - not total distance covered.

"[Some] teams that do not run a lot get very good results because they have [their] way of playing."

Sprints matter more than distance covered for Iraola's side, who have clear ideas of how to press, looking to win the ball back through a sudden and intense pressure from familiar positions they are well prepared for.

If the conditions to implement this press aren't on, the wingers can be seen dropping off, forming a more compact defensive shape with the likes of Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz defending in a front two for longer periods of the match.

It's smart. Liverpool look to maximise the effectiveness of when they do press, with full commitment expected in each sprint, with players conserving their energy in moments a press is less likely to succeed.

With pressing being a front-footed idea, coaches may throw caution to the wind but this can leave them exposed in ways teams have become better at exploiting.

Hurzeler touched on the need for balance when pressing.

"I always say in certain moments you need to have the courage to take risk but you need to have the discipline to control the risk," he said.

For Brighton, this looks like certain players abandoning man-to-man marking when their respective attacker attempts to drag them into awkward positions.

Instead, Brighton will protect the centre of the pitch on top of their man-to-man principles which helps them stay compact.

In yellow, we can see the man-oriented defence of Brighton against Arsenal. The players highlighted in white are taking a more central position designed to protect dangerous areas of the pitch. This is an example of how impressive coaches are combining man-to-man pressing with zonal ideas

When the defending side aren't compact, spaces exist for the attacking side to target. When players step up to press, these gaps can arise in between the lines.

Again, Brighton manage to plug these gaps well by pressing hard, reducing the time opponents have to play passes into midfield, while also encouraging players to make vertical jumps up the pitch, covering players left by teammates who have pressed higher up the pitch.

As Declan Rice passes the ball backwards, Brighton's players press forward, locking on to the player in front of them

Chema Andres recognises that Bruno Guimaraes has been left unmarked in midfield so makes a vertical jump, closing him down, and ensuring Brighton remain compact

When teams lack vertical compactness - not pressing with enough intensity and without making the necessary steps up the pitch - the space left in midfield has been exploited by clever sides, such as Leeds.

In their 4-1 loss to Daniel Farke's men, Chelsea looked to press high, with attackers and midfielders running up the pitch to apply pressure.

But when the ball went back the other way, these same players struggled.

The idea behind playing over a team's press isn't always to make the ball stick at the feet of a target man, although this helps. Instead space is found in the gaps between the pressing side's lines.

Recognising when teammates are likely to win headers or clip the ball forwards, midfielders are able to turn and run in the direction the ball is heading in, positioned ready to win second balls in numbers.

By comparison, the pressing side's midfielders, having to apply forward pressure before turning around to track back are often slower to contest second balls.

Chelsea play a long goal-kick towards Leeds' back line. This forward pass brings with it the forward pressure of Chelsea's attackers and midfielders. The Leeds' defender heads it back, against the direction of Chelsea's press

Leeds' midfielders have oriented themselves well to form a net around where the ball may drop. The Chelsea midfielders and attackers, starting from further away and having to turn around, aren't well placed to contest for the loose ball

The same ideas are seen again. The Leeds' midfielder, under insufficient pressure, is able to play the ball forward quickly. This catches Chelsea's midfield line high up the pitch. Chelsea's Romeo Lavia has to turn before he can get back into position whilst Leeds attacking midfielders are closer to the ball, facing forwards

This allows Leeds to exploit the space between Chelsea's lines

By this point, it will be clear that pressing is influenced by countless variables but it is worth highlighting one final factor; teams need solutions when pressing with one fewer player than the attacking side.

This most obviously happens when the opposition goalkeeper is involved in build-up play.

Here, the team in possession have 11 options against the 10 pressing players.

Obvious solutions come in the form one of the forward attackers pressing a centre-back at an angle which usually forces them to pass it back to the goalkeeper.

At that point, the same pressing player will continue his run, now pressing the keeper.

By curving their run and pressing at an angle, the idea is that the keeper will struggle to pass it back to the now unmarked centre-back.

This is generally true but again, good teams have found smart solutions to access this player.

Charalampos Kostoulas first presses Gabriel Magalhaes, who passes the ball to his keeper, David Raya. Kostoulas then curves his run, blocking off Raya's pass back to Gabriel

One solution comes when the keeper passes the ball into a central player who then bounces the pass into the unmarked centre-back. This comes with risk given that the central player is usually marked. But sudden darts towards the ball can give them the time and space to play the bounce pass required.

Under some pressure, Rice darts towards the ball, gaining some separation from his marker. He gestures for the ball knowing he can play a first time pass to Gabriel who is unmarked

What happens instead is Raya, under immense pressure, defaults to playing long. His pass ends up out of play.

A riskier but more impressive solution is when the keeper is willing and able to avoid the opponents attempt to force him in one direction, instead playing the ball back the other way themselves.

Queens Park Rangers' Pierce Charles, on loan from Manchester City, has done this better than most in world football, and his quality was clearest against Swansea's excellent press.

By playing against the direction of Swansea's press, to his unmarked teammate, he was able to immediately disorganise their press.

QPR's right-sided defender passes the ball back to Charles. The Swansea striker, first pressing the defender, angles his body to discourage Charles from playing back to the unmarked player. He closes Charles down as he does this

Swansea's press is designed to force Charles to his left but he bravely plays back the other way

By finding the unmarked man on the other side in space, Swansea have to reorganise their defensive shape

Changes in how a team presses force teams to innovate their build-up play which in turn force teams to innovate in how they press. It's a cycle that spins at a blistering pace, especially in the Premier League.

Given the detailed analysis and constant adaptation, teams and coaches in 2026 can ill-afford to rest on their laurels.

#874. What is the Riemann hypothesis? A guide to the famed conjecture that rules prime numbers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

German mathematician Bernhard Riemann formulated his famous conjecture in 1859.Credit: Smithsonian Libraries and Archives (CC0)

On 20 November, mathematicians made two competing announcements about solving the Riemann hypothesis — perhaps the most important open problem in mathematics.

The question had remained unanswered since it was formulated in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann (1826–66). His statement is central to the theory of prime numbers, the whole numbers that cannot be evenly divided by any other number except themselves or 1.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The hypothesis concerns the distribution of primes, and it is important because these numbers are central to all of maths. “There is nothing more basic and more fundamental in mathematics that the prime numbers,” says Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, a mathematician at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.

Riemann arrived at his idea by studying prime numbers as waves — in a way that presages the way music recordings are compressed into mp3 files — and his hypothesis is usually described in abstruse-sounding language. But at its heart, the idea boils down to a statistical test that is familiar to any scientist who’s ever analysed data.

Nature breaks down the Riemann hypothesis.

Mathematicians want to know how predictable the prime numbers are. The German scientist Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), who many consider to be the greatest mathematician in history, had noticed in the late eighteenth century (when he was a teenager) that if you pick any whole number, the odds that it’s a prime depend on the number’s size. Primes slowly become sparser as numbers become bigger. Gauss observed that their frequency seems to depend on (or, is inversely proportional to) the number of digits. Roughly speaking, among numbers with k digits, one in every k of them is a prime.

In Riemann’s time, a half-century after Gauss’s guess, there was still no rigorous proof of this. In a landmark paper in 1859, Riemann stated his belief that the late Gauss, who had been one of his mentors at the University of Göttingen, had been right.

But Riemann — who was a “daring” thinker, says maths historian Rossana Tazzioli at the University of Lille in France — went much further. He proposed that Gauss’s “one in every k” guess was a good statistical prediction, meaning that the frequency of the primes should not fluctuate away from it too much. In other words, Riemann made a guess about the margin of error of Gauss’s prediction.

If true, this ‘Riemann hypothesis’ would make primes’ behaviour similar to that of a random process, such as a series of coin tosses. More precisely, he suggested that when you count the primes among the first n whole numbers, fluctuations would take a form that many scientists are familiar with: “The idea of the Riemann hypothesis is that the error term looks a lot like √n, which is what any random model will give you,” says Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Such square-root terms pop up everywhere in data analysis, because they control the shrinking of a margin of error as the number n of data points grows.

In his paper, Riemann did much more than guess. He introduced tools that would constitute the basis for much of the work on number theory — the branch of mathematics that concerns integers, primes and divisibility — in the following centuries.

First, by developing new techniques in analysis — another word for advanced calculus — as he went along, Riemann constructed the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter ‘zeta’).

Riemann then showed that the function embodied an enormous amount of information about prime numbers. First, he proved that the solutions to the equation ζ (z) = 0 — where z is a point on a plane — encode the statistical distribution of prime numbers along the number line. To do so, Riemann employed a type of Fourier analysis, the type of maths that nowadays enables the compression of music into compact mp3 files by breaking sound waves down into sinusoidal components.

#873. What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​

The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

#872. Syrian referee refutes ‘drunk’ accusations as ‘insult and defamation’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Syrian referee Hanna Hattab was replaced at half-time of the AFC Champions League Two match between Gol Gohar and Al Jazira

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A referee has hit back at claims he was “drunk” while officiating an AFC Champions League Two match.

Footage has been widely shared on social media of Syrian referee Hanna Hattab looking visibly disoriented during a match between Iran's Gol Gohar and Al Jazira of the United Arab Emirates.

One particular incident raised eyebrows when Hattab showed a yellow card to Al Jazira’s goalkeeper for a foul that happened close to the halfway line, 40 yards away from him.

Hattab was then replaced at half-time with the fourth official taking over for the remainder of the game, which Al Jazira won 1-0.

Reports claimed Gol Gohar staff accused the referee of being drunk following erratic decision-making as similar accusations flooded in online.

But Hattab, who is part of the AFC's elite refereeing group, has refuted the allegations as “insult and defamation”, threatening legal action.

“I also confirm my full right to take all legal and judicial measures against anyone who published or made a statement or contributed to the insult and defamation of me, regardless of their position or status, whether they are an individual, an institution, or a sports entity.”

He also said he would issue a further statement following contact with the Syrian Arab Football Federation (SFA) which will “clarify all the details and facts related to what happened ... with full transparency and clarity.”

Omani journalist Issa Said, who covers Asian football, has since claimed on social media that what happened to Hattab was "due to a drop in his blood sugar, which caused him to lose concentration and focus".

The SFA have also put out a statement standing in support of Hattab, while stating it has requested his medical report from the match.

“The Main Referees Committee of the Syrian Arab Football Federation confirms that it stands in full support of international referee Mr Hana Khattab regarding the incident he was subjected to, following reassurance about his health,” it said.

“This comes after the committee was reassured of his well-being, following a number of discussions on social media concerning the incident. The committee emphasises its full support for him and its commitment to following up on the matter in all its details and developments.

“In this regard, the committee has requested that the Syrian Football Referees Committee provide the medical report relating to the referee, the match observers' report and the referee assessor's report. This is in order to establish the circumstances of the incident accurately and comprehensively and to complete the necessary procedures in this matter.

“The committee also confirms that it will provide the relevant authorities and the public with the findings as soon as the requested reports are received, in order to ensure accuracy and to obtain information from official sources.”

#869. Europa League match suspended after police clashes over Palestine banner

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The game, being played on neutral ground in Batumi, Georgia, was halted in the 26th minute and restarted 30 minutes later

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Europa League game between Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva was suspended for around 30 minutes on Thursday when police clashed with fans of the Turkish club after they displayed a banner in support of Palestine.

The game, being played on neutral ground in Batumi, Georgia, was halted in the 26th minute but restarted after the interruption.

Turkey’s Haberturk broadcaster said Georgian police used pepper spray against the Besiktas fans, who also unfurled a Palestinian flag, prompting referee referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0-0.

In a statement, Besiktas accused the Georgian security forces of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game.

Georgian police entered the stands and ⁠used pepper spray on Besiktas fans, Turkish outlet NTV reported.

“We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the club said. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.”

The report added that Turkish fans chanted “Down with Israel” and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters before play restarted to calm the situation.

The Turkish Football Federation condemned the treatment of Besiktas supporters on X, saying they were subjected to unacceptable behaviour and discrimination. It said it would press for an investigation.

The TFF’s statement read: “We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, conduct and interference directed at Beşiktaş supporters, both inside and outside the stadium, before and during our club’s Uefa Europa League match against Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia.

“No practice that disregards the universal values of sport, human dignity, mutual respect and the principles of fair play, or that involves discrimination, exclusion or security failures, can be tolerated.

“Nor can there be any question of remaining silent in the face of such conduct, which endangers our supporters’ safety and targets their fundamental rights and freedoms.

“As the Turkish Football Federation, we declare unequivocally that we will follow this matter to its conclusion to ensure that the events are fully investigated, those responsible are identified and the necessary sanctions are imposed without delay.

“There must be no tolerance for covering up these events, allowing those responsible to evade accountability or permitting similar violations to recur.

“We emphasize that we stand firmly with our club, Besiktas, and our supporters, who faced a series of problems, particularly serious security failures, and extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our supporters subjected to interference and mistreatment.

“Let no one forget that we will not remain silent in the face of disrespect, discrimination and security violations directed at representatives and supporters of Turkish football.

“We will act decisively on national and international platforms to ensure that all necessary steps are taken, particularly with Uefa, and that those responsible are held accountable.”

Turkish clubs echoed the sentiments of the TFF, with Besiktas’ rivals Fenerbahce, Galatasaray and Trabzonspor all among those to stand with the club.

“We do not accept Turkish clubs being denied the right to play their home matches in their own country, in front of their own fans, when facing clubs from the occupying state of Israel,” Trabzonspor wrote in a statement.

“We do not consider Uefa’s double standards on this issue acceptable. We also strongly condemn the disproportionate intervention by security forces against Besiktas fans in Georgia this evening.”

The ⁠officiating team and the Besiktas players ‌left ​the pitch before ‌the game restarted.

Earlier, the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported.

Hapoel Beer-Sheva and Israel FA had not commented on the incident at the time of publishing.

#868. NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth

When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into interstellar space continues.

Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

Manchester United are in the market for a central defender and Mauricio Pochettino understands the need better than most

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sunday’s bruising 4-0 defeat at Anfield exposed the scale of the rebuild facing Mauricio Pochettino at Manchester United.

For all the scrutiny aimed at Man United’s midfield and attack, it is the fragility at the back that is of greatest concern - the club have now conceded more goals than any other side in Europe's top five leagues this season.

With the January transfer window fast approaching, Fulham’s Calvin Bassey - often linked with an Old Trafford move - is rapidly playing himself into contention for a switch.

Man United’s need for centre-half reinforcements could hardly be more urgent after the weekend's display. Matthijs de Ligt looked worryingly off the pace against Liverpool, struggling with his turning circle and repeatedly caught out whenever Andoni Iraola's side broke at speed.

The long-term picture looks increasingly bleak, too. Lisandro Martinez is widely expected to move on at the end of the season after previously speaking out publicly against the club, leaving a left-footed vacancy at the heart of defence.

Across the rest of Pochettino’s central defensive options, there is a lack of ready-made solutions. Leny Yoro, who endured a miserable afternoon of his own on Merseyside, and Ayden Heaven are both still very junior in their development, while Harry Maguire isn't getting any younger.

Throwing teenagers and early-20-somethings into an Old Trafford pressure cooker every week is no recipe for climbing the table, nor can Man United rely indefinitely on an ageing veteran to bail them out, as Maguire has done so consistently in the past.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That is why Bassey ticks so many boxes for Man United’s new era under Pochettino.

Turning 27 on New Year’s Eve, the Nigeria international is entering his prime years as a defender. And having racked up more than 100 Premier League appearances since arriving in west London from Ajax in 2023, he brings the sort of battle-hardened top-flight pedigree Man United are crying out for.

In doing so, he removes the adaptation risk that has plagued so many overseas Old Trafford arrivals. His commanding display in Fulham’s 1-1 draw away at Manchester City on Saturday makes the appeal obvious; Bassey has good recovery pace, is dominant in physical duels, and comfortable defending wide channels.

Bassey won't cost the earth either as his initial four-year contract at Craven Cottage expires next summer, and although Fulham hold an option to extend his stay by a further 12 months, his contractual situation keeps any potential fee firmly within reach for a club of Man United's stature and commercial acumen.

Fulham are understandably eager to tie him down to fresh terms, but the lure of spearheading Pochettino’s Old Trafford reboot may prove hard to resist.

In FourFourTwo's view, if Bassey maintains his current level over the coming weeks, don't rule out a January approach.

Newcastle United star Sven Botman has been banned from driving after he was caught using his mobile phone at the wheel.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) confirmed that Botman, 26, pleaded guilty at Newcastle Magistrates Court on Wednesday.

The Dutch international defender was given six penalty points and disqualified from driving for six months, as these were added to points he had already accrued.

The MoJ said Botman was fined £900 and ordered to pay £400 costs and a £360 surcharge.

Court documents show that Botman was in a Land Rover on the A189 Haddricks Mill Road, in Newcastle, on 17 September when he was spotted using his phone.

According to The Sun, the court heard he was filmed by a cyclist while he was stationary in traffic.

The Dutch centre-half was signed by Newcastle in a £32 million deal from French club Lille during the summer of 2022.

Since signing for the Magpies, Botman has made 124 appearances and was part of the squad that won the League Cup in 2025, their first major trophy in decades.

#864. EFL preview: Happy Potters face struggling Hammers

Mark Robins (left) has Stoke where Scott Parker (right) would love to take West Ham

You've dug the de-icer and novelty jumpers out the back of the cupboard and within days a square of chocolate before breakfast will be socially acceptable again.

December is looming large, but you can be sure the season of goodwill does not extend to the English Football League.

There are furious battles raging at the top and bottom of the Championship, League One and League Two with more than a third of the campaign in the rear-view mirror and a huge month coming up which might just determine who will be on the naughty or nice list in 2027.

Here are five things to look out for across the EFL before the advent calendars are opened.

'Massive for both' - Saints and Boro revisit Spygate rivalry

If, as they say, seven days is a long time in football, then seven months feels like a lifetime.

In April, West Ham were trying to maintain a two-point cushion over Tottenham in the Premier League relegation scrap, while Stoke were careering down the Championship table. A run of one point from their final six matches saw them finish 17th.

On Saturday, they meet at the London Stadium (15:00 GMT) with the Potters 11 points and 11 places above the Hammers in this season's Championship standings.

Tuesday's defeat at Portsmouth means Scott Parker has taken just two points from four games since replacing Nuno Espirito Santo at the helm in east London, with his side now winless in six games.

The Hammers slipped into the bottom half of the table following Wednesday's results â the Irons have not finished lower than eighth in the second tier since 1956.

By contrast Mark Robins has led Stoke to five straight wins.

The 2-1 victory against Millwall on Wednesday means they have taken an incredible 35 points from their past 14 games, having begun the season with three straight losses.

A sixth win in a row might be enough to see Stoke take over at the top, given leaders Middlesbrough play at Southampton on Friday night, while a seventh game without a win could leave the Hammers closer to the relegation zone than the promotion places.

Unthinkable for the pre-season title favourites, and with six of their seven games before the turn of the year against sides scrapping for the automatic promotion spots or play-off places, this could just be the start of a bleak winter for the Irons.

As far as claret and blue teams freshly relegated from the Premier League go, West Ham have got it pretty good compared to Burnley.

Wednesday's 2-0 defeat by Birmingham at Turf Moor made it an English record 24 games without a home win, a run stretching back to October 2025.

Overall, the Clarets have won just one of their past 29 league games dating back to February - a 4-0 triumph at Watford on 10 October.

Fabio Celestini's side are second-bottom, a point above Derby, and could sink to the foot of the table if they fail to win at Millwall on Saturday (15:00 GMT).

Wednesday's 2-1 defeat at Stoke was a fourth straight defeat for Alex Neil's side who have taken just 12 points from their past 15 games, losing nine of them.

Pretty incredible seeing as how the Lions lost just 11 across the whole of last season, when they finished third, and might well have found themselves in the division above the Clarets this season, had things turned out differently in their play-off semi-final against Hull City.

Edward Iordanescu was in the stand for Watford's midweek home defeat by Blackburn

The game at The Den is not the only intriguing one in the second tier this Saturday as new basement-boys Derby welcome crisis club Watford to Pride Park (15:00 GMT).

The Rams have taken two steps back after taking one forward, picking up their only win in their past 13 games when they beat Bolton at home on 6 November.

They lost 2-0 to Southampton last weekend and 3-0 at Wolves on Tuesday in a game where they allowed 39 shots on their goal - the most by any side in the Championship in 11 years.

Preston North End's resurgence has left the Rams bottom of the pile with 35 goals conceded in 17 matches - the worst in the second tier along with Burnley.

They welcome a Hornets side who are 20th, three points above the drop-zone, after Wednesday's 1-0 home defeat to Blackburn, before which the players met new boss Edward Iordanescu for the first time.

The Romanian certainly has a big task on his hands, Watford have taken a single point from eight away games and were thumped 4-0 at Sheffield United last Saturday in Alessio Dionisi's last stand, while they now haven't scored in three games overall.

We are going to find out an awful lot about Sheffield Wednesday's prospects in League One in the next three weeks.

Dave Challinor's arrival has seemingly steadied the ship, but a stalemate at Stevenage on Tuesday was a sideways step after back-to-back wins over Plymouth and Barnsley in which Wednesday rode their luck at times.

The Owls are fourth, five points off the top, and unbeaten in five, but have played a game more than most sides around them and face in-form promotion rivals Oxford United, Leicester and Luton in the run-up to Christmas after Saturday's visit of Reading (15:00 GMT).

The Royals have slipped to ninth after a run of one point from a possible 12, losing their past three and taking only six points from eight away games, with just one win.

They will be desperate to return to the play-off race and end their slump, and if they can do it the pressure will be firmly on Wednesday in the weeks to come.

In the past 14 seasons they have been promoted or relegated in 10 of them, but Millers fans will be keen for just a season of stability given the way things have started following the drop from League One last season.

An eight-match winless run has left Alex Bruce's Millers second-bottom, only off the foot of the EFL by virtue of scoring more than Crawley, level on points and goal difference - pretty incredible for a club which has spent more seasons in the Championship (seven) than anywhere else since they were last in the fourth tier in 2013.

They will seek to end their slide with Bruce sat in the stands on Saturday (15:00 GMT) when they host Oldham, a side who were mid-table in the National League when the Millers began their last Championship campaign, but now sit three points better off in 20th.

Rotherham actually picked up a creditable goalless draw at Grimsby last weekend, which denied the Mariners a place in the automatic promotion spots.

Fourth-placed Town will seek to put that right when they head to Crewe, two places behind on goal difference alone, this weekend, in a crazy division where just four points separate Grimsby from Fleetwood in 15th.

You can follow the entire EFL weekend as it happens here on the BBC Sport website and app, starting with live text coverage of Southampton v Middlesbrough on Friday, 27 November.
