#757. Has AI just cracked Internet encryption? Rumoured ‘bombshell’ stuns scientists

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from online banking and private messages to sensitive government communications.Credit: Peshkov/Getty

Artificial-intelligence agents have already begun to wreak havoc by hacking into servers around the world, either spontaneously or directed by humans. Now, a threat is emerging that is on a whole other scale.

Several computer scientists have suggested on social media that the leading AI laboratories — companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, both in San Francisco, California — have discovered algorithms that could derail the security of Internet communications.

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs

“I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells,” computer scientist Scott Aaronson wrote yesterday on his blog. The details are still hazy, added Aaronson, who is at the University of Texas at Austin. “Until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells.”

The algorithms are rumoured to target the information-scrambling system known as RSA, which relies on the mathematics of prime numbers, as well as more-advanced technologies.

While the rumours could not be confirmed, other breakthroughs announced by the AI companies this week make researchers cautiously optimistic that the mathematics of encryption could eventually come to help.

Nature examines the threat, and what can be done about it.

Several researchers say they have heard that some of the leading AI laboratories have discovered algorithms capable of breaking public-key cryptography in ‘polynomial time’ (or ‘P’ in computer-science shorthand).

Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from banking apps to Internet browsers. It relies on mathematical problems that are considered practically impossible for computers to solve within a reasonable amount of time.

An algorithm that could solve these problems in polynomial time would change that. It means the time needed to solve a problem would increase relatively slowly as the problem gets larger. For example, a password of length n could be broken in a number of steps proportional to the square or cube of its size (n² or n³).

The race to save the Internet from quantum hackers

The race to save the Internet from quantum hackers

Theoretical computer scientists tend to think of P problems as relatively easy to solve, especially compared with problems that require exponential time, where the number of steps might grow as 2n, for example. As n gets larger — or a password gets longer — the time required by an exponential algorithm quickly exceeds that of any polynomial one.

In practical terms, an algorithm that could break public-key cryptography in polynomial time could undermine much of the security on which the Internet relies.

It depends on which encryption systems they could crack, and how efficiently they could do so.

One of the most ubiquitous techniques for establishing public keys is to multiply two large prime numbers. This technique, called RSA, was long believed to be secure because ‘cracking the code’ requires factoring that product back into the original primes, a much slower process (at least, without a powerful quantum computer, which does not yet exist). One of the rumours now circulating is that the AI labs have found an algorithm that can do this.

But even though a polynomial-time algorithm could be very powerful on paper, it could still be impossible to use except for the shortest passwords. An algorithm requiring n10000steps, for example, be very impractical to apply.

However, proving that a problem is in ‘P’, even if the polynomial-time solution is practically useless, has usually been followed by improvements that have eventually led to efficient solutions. “The issue is that the idea that [the problem] was hard — because of needing exponential time — is dead,” Aaronson tells Nature.

Not necessarily. This type of worst-case scenario hinges on a long-standing open question known as ‘P = NP’: could every problem whose solution can be checked in polynomial time also be solved in polynomial time? If so, problems that underpin essentially all public-key cryptography could become much easier to crack.

Quantum-computing pioneer warns of complacency over Internet security

Quantum-computing pioneer warns of complacency over Internet security

But most researchers think that this is unlikely. In fact, some recent AI-aided results have made them cautiously optimistic. Earlier this week, both Anthropic and OpenAI announced results in theoretical computer science that suggest that many similar problems could be hard to solve. Before the recent explosion in AI-aided maths, each of those advances would have been hailed as the computer-science breakthrough of the decade, Aaronson says.

Ryan Williams, a computer scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, agrees. “I am definitely blown away by the latest developments.” One especially interesting result, he says, shows that for a ubiquitous type of computation called matrix multiplication, the exponent in a polynomial-time algorithm cannot be too small. “Underneath the hood, it seems to provide a brand-new framework for proving limitations on efficient computation,” says Williams.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03875-6

#756. Taylor says he is quitting darts for good after comeback

Phil Taylor retired from professional darts in 2018; he came out of retirement for this week's MODUS Super Series International Pairs, teaming up with friend Adrian Lewis; the Pair finished second-bottom in group C and were knocked out of the event

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Phil Taylor says he is quitting competitive darts for good and has no plans to come out of retirement again.

The 16-time world champion was lured back to the oche for this year's MODUS Super Series International Pairs Tournament in Portsmouth alongside his long-time friend Adrian Lewis.

The English duo lost all five of their matches on Thursday but rebounded on Friday, winning three and losing two matches, to finish second-bottom in the Group C standings.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Taylor, 67, retired from the competitive circuit in 2018, five years after winning his final world crown, and when asked if he would make another comeback, the 14-time PDC World Championship winner told Pluto TV: "[This is] proper retirement."

A heartwarming moment unfolded after Taylor and Lewis were beaten 4-3 in their final group match against Scotland, as each of the other nations arrived to give Taylor a guard of honour, as he walked away from the oche.

"I mean I'm 67, I get my pension next February," Taylor said, when asked if this would be his last competitive appearance. "I'm a pensioner now, officially!"

"I'll still do personal appearances, more having a chat with people, talking about my career, that kind of thing."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Taylor and Lewis, who teamed up to win four World Cup of Darts titles between 2012 and 2016, finished Thursday at the bottom of Group C. Friday started poorly for the Englishmen, losing to Denmark's Ivan Springborg-Poulsen and Andreas Toft Jørgensen 4-2.

Speaking on his retirement U-turn this week, Taylor said: "I was dreading it to be honest with you because I know I wasn't playing like I can do, but now I've been here and it's all over, I've loved it."

The pair hit back on Friday with a 4-3 win against Germany, then beat Switzerland and Sweden, both 4-2.

The Englishmen would tie Scotland at three legs apiece in his final competitive match, before Taylor missed a checkout for 48 for victory, in what would have been a fairy-tale finish.

"Looking back now, it's like it never happened," Taylor said, reflecting on his glittering career.

"I've said to other people who have been on stage and retired: 'How do you feel now?'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"'It's like you've never been there'. It's ever so weird. And you come up on YouTube and you just go: "No, I know. I know I was there, but I can't remember it."

"It's very, very strange because, mentally-wise, you move on. That was your former life and now my life is different."

Instead of flying around the world competing, Taylor says retirement has allowed him to spend more time with his grandchildren.

"I've got 11 grandchildren," Taylor said. "So I spend a lot of time with them now.

"[I do] things I've never done before. Go to bed when I want; I go to bed early. For me, 9pm would be like, I'd be asleep two hours before 9pm, and it's great.

"I love getting up early as well. We can do all the chores. We can go shopping and get everything done, and it isn't even 11am. It's great!

"People say I'm the GOAT [Greatest of All Time]-I'm an old goat now!"

Arsenal co-chairman Josh Kroenke should probably turn his phone off if the Gunners fall behind against Manchester City on Sunday.

Chris Sutton's predictions guest this week, Kings of Leon drummer and City fan Nathan Followill, is good friends with Kroenke - and says he will be in touch if the game is going City's way.

"I'm super excited for this weekend and I've got my smack talk ready for Josh already," Followill told BBC Sport.

"I've heard about the City fans with their inflatable bananas and I need to get myself one. My wife is going to be like 'er, an inflatable banana just arrived in the mail - do you know anything about that?'

Chris Sutton and Nathan Followill were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

You can never rule City out because of Haaland's ability to score goals but the only result I see here is an Arsenal win, and I am going for a classic Gunners scoreline.

Nathan's prediction: This is the big one! It's huge. I feel really good about it, too. Arsenal are riding so high at the moment, I feel like we might catch them snoozing.

I predict Haaland will get two goals, Phil Foden will get one too and we will end up with four. 2-4

After drawing a blank since week two, Chris finally picked up another win in week 11 - and it was his spot-on prediction for Liverpool to thump Manchester United 4-0 that sealed the deal.

That meant he got three correct results, including two exact scores - at Anfield, and Tottenham's 2-0 win over Ipswich - giving him a total of 90 points.

In a tricky week for predictions, where Liverpool were the only team to start the weekend in the Premier League's top six who won, it was those exact scores that made all the difference.

Chris' guest, undisputed world champion boxer Lauren Price, the BBC readers and AI also all got three correct results.

But the BBC readers were the only ones to also get an exact score - in the Spurs game - giving them 60 points.

Lauren and AI both ended up on 30 points - AI did call Newcastle's draw with Arsenal correctly, but it was wrong about Bournemouth's win over Nottingham Forest, which everyone else got right.

Not many of you got that Liverpool-United scoreline correct, either.

From around 27,000 predictions, the most popular scoreline picked was a 2-1 home win and only 570 of you went for 4-0.

"When has AI ever gone for a 4-0?" said Sutton. "That's what the crowd wants. The crowd don't want AI - who wants mathematics?

"The crowd want gut-feeling and instinct. I think I should get 1,000 points for that prediction, because I was brave enough to go for it."

For the first time this season, there were SIX games where no-one made a correct prediction - who thought it was easy?

The biggest shock of the week was Leeds' 4-1 victory at Stamford Bridge. Again from around 27,000 predictions, more than 3,600 (14%) of you did back Daniel Farke's side to win... but just 11 of you saw that scoreline coming.

#753. No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal

One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.

Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.

The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.

This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating issues such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.

The text still includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that was pushed by host Turkey.

It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources rather than fossil fuels, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries.

The draft did mention the electrification target alongside efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally as well as other energy efficiency measures. But Jan Kowalzig, a climate finance expert with Oxfam Germany, said negotiators had failed to "meaningfully" link them.

Kowalzig also criticized the text for not referencing a transition away from fossil fuels in a gradual manner — something that had been mentioned in the final decision out of the COP28 in Dubai several years ago.

"This is insufficient for a climate conference that already decided several years ago to phase out fossil fuels and that presents itself as a conference focused on implementation," he said in a statement.

Another hotly contested issue at the talks has been financial support to help developing countries deal with climate change. Divisions largely revolve around who should bear the costs and whether funding should come in the form of grants or loans.

The second draft called for further discussions on a tripling of funding for climate adaptation measures in developing countries. It also noted "with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs," with the adaptation costs in developing countries estimated at $305 billion annually up to 2035.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The wording on finance prompted criticism from Meenakshi Raman, the coordinator of the climate change program at the Third World Network, who had been "hoping to see much more ambition on the side of finance from the developed world."

"Coming here really confirmed the worst fears that developed countries are not only backsliding but putting nothing in terms of real meaning on the table," said Raman.

The European Union has said it won't agree to higher climate financing pledges because it pays its "fair share" while others don't.

The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.

It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems."

Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the text aimed to communicate that "1.5 degrees of warming is not acceptable and will not be allowed to stand."

The draft also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane.

The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up, many of which have yet to be tested and proven on a large scale.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries said the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community."

The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run on for longer than expected. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.

Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.

On Thursday, Panama said it would block any agreement that does not meet its demands for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate methane.

The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said Panama would "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.

Australian Energy Minister Bowen said he expected countries to bring forward their concerns, feedback and questions in the coming hours and overnight.

"We won't be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus, until we have a plan we can put to the parties on behalf of the countries and governments they represent, and they can say, yes, we can do this: we can keep the world to 1.5 degrees of warming."

The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.

The conference is the first to be held under the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.

Countries are at odds about how to acknowledge overshoot of the temperature threshold in the final agreement, with some worrying that fossil fuel producing countries such as Saudi Arabia and Iran are seeking to jettison 1.5C entirely, which could lead to "backsliding" on climate action, according to AFP.

"It's critically important for this COP to recognize, and this is really the first COP that will likely do so, that we are on the way to overshooting 1.5 degrees," said David Waskow, the director of the World Resources Institute's International Climate Initiative.

#752. Paige DeSorbo Goes Social Media Official With Boyfriend Joe D’Amelio

Paige DeSorbo debuted her romance with boyfriend Joe D'Amelio on TikTok Nov. 25 nearly two years after the couple first sparked romance rumors.

Paige DeSorbo is serving up a hard launch.

Four months after the Summer House alum denied rumors that she and boyfriend Joe D’Amelio got engaged, she made their romance social media official, sharing a funny video on TikTok of her friends making homemade pizzas.

As DeSorbo captioned the Nov. 25 TikTok video, which she also shared on her Instagram Stories, “We aren’t Italian at all.”

The clip featured the Giggly Squad podcast host’s pals cooking up pies and hanging out as they lip-synced to audio from a scene from the 1990 classic Goodfellas, in which Henry Hill (Ray Liotta) introduces the members of mafia capo Paulie Cicero’s crew.

“There was Jimmy, and Tommy, and me. And there was Anthony Stabile, Frankie Carbone,” Liotta’s Hill says in the scene. “And then there was Mo Black’s brother, Fat Andy and his guys, Frankie the Wop and Freddy No Nose. And then there was Pete the Killer, who was Sally Balls’ brother. Then you had Nickey Eyes and Mikey Franzese.”

And among the family and friends who made a cameo in DeSorbo’s video was D’Amelio, who lifted up his drink in greeting as the camera panned to him during the “Nickey Eyes” line.

While the couple first sparked romance rumors way back in February 2025, they have kept their relationship offline until now. And fans couldn’t help but get excited about the update.

“GIRRRRRRRRL it’s tiktok official okayyy honey,” one user wrote in the comments section of DeSorbo’s video, while another added, “Paige he’s so handsome and fits in so well I’m so happy for you kween.”

Although this marks the D’Amelio’s debut on DeSorbo’s social media, the Bravo alum previously shared insight into their romance, joking to Us Weekly in a February interview that while Italian men have a reputation for being “not quiet,” she’s found that’s not the case.

“They’re quiet. And I appreciate that,” she quipped. “They know when to speak and when not to, and that’s important. That’s important in a man—know when to shut it.”

#751. Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?

Russian President Putin has suggested evacuating civilians from the embattled Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka. But experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.

Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.

In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."

Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.

Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

#750. 'A bit strange' - Leclerc seeking outlier to catch Mercedes in Qatar

Mercedes dominated Friday's practice sessions at the Qatar Grand Prix and Charles Leclerc suggested Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull are missing something; watch final practice at 2.30pm ahead of Qualifying at 6pm on Saturday live on Sky Sports F1

Sports Journalist @NigelCJourno

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Charles Leclerc believes an “outlier” has given Mercedes a “massive” advantage at the Qatar Grand Prix, after Kimi Antonelli and George Russell dominated Friday’s practice sessions.

Mercedes were nearly half a second quicker than the rest of the field at the Lusail International Circuit as Antonelli topped both sessions from Russell.

Their four-tenths advantage over closest challenger Lando Norris in second practice could have been even greater, with neither Antonelli nor Russell completing a full low-fuel lap on the soft tyres. It was an ominous sign for the rest of the field ahead of Saturday's qualifying, which gets under way at 6pm, with coverage live on Sky Sports F1 from 5.15pm.

Mercedes' dominance was similar to their pace advantage earlier in the season but the second half of 2026 has largely been very close between F1's top four teams - Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull and McLaren.

Ferrari were over one second behind Antonelli on a dismal Friday as Leclerc spun in second practice and Lewis Hamilton suffered an engine problem which brought his Ferrari to a halt.

"Honestly it's been a very difficult day. It's not that we didn't try on the softs, we couldn't improve our lap time on the mediums," said Leclerc.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I lost the car and had some damage so we had to repair the car but that was the first lap of FP2 and I couldn't improve and even on the new soft later on I couldn't improve.

"A very, very difficult day. The feeling is just very difficult to get right. Not even on high fuel we were strong, so for now, it looks like a very difficult weekend but we are working hard to try and understand something.

"For some reason, Mercedes are so much faster than everybody expected, so the gaps are just a little bit strange, so there's something that's an outlier and we just need to find that."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Ferrari were not expected to be strong at the Lusail International Circuit due to the long flat out zones and high-speed corners but Leclerc suggested his team, along with McLaren and Red Bull were missing a trick that will give them more pace.

"I don't think we know yet what's the outlier. I think other teams probably didn't find that because Mercedes still have a massive advantage," he said.

"We are going to work towards that and analyse the data to understand what's going on."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

McLaren were predicted to be very competitive in Qatar due to their strength in the high-speed corners but Norris and Piastri were never close to matching the pace of Mercedes.

On Saturday, McLaren are expected to put the new floor they ran in Las Vegas on the car but Norris does not think it will make a big enouch difference to catch Mercedes who are in "a different category".

"I don't know how much that will help around here compared to Vegas," said last year's world champion.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"But obviously tonight [Friday] we will see how much we can gain from that. It's not going to be the gap we need.

"We are probably seven tenths off the Mercedes a lap so it's not even worth thinking about them. But relative to the rest we seem to be in a good place. The fact we can have the new floor on tomorrow will add a little bit and a little bit is better than nothing. We seem in a relatively decent place."

Both Antonelli and Russell pointed out that Verstappen will always be a threat and the four-time world champion is coy about his chances of challenging the Mercedes in qualifying.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"A bit of a difficult day. The balance of the car is a bit too disconnected at the moment to go fast, so that's what we need to fix," said the Red Bull driver.

"The all-round balance is not there at the moment and is costing us quite a bit of lap time. We will keep trying and see how good we can get it."

"Mercedes look quite far ahead on the short run and long run. Let's see how much we can close the gap."

#747. The Best Thanksgiving TV Episodes and Movies to Binge Right Now

Gossip Girl, The O.C. and Gilmore Girls are just some of our favorite shows that served up more than just portions on Thanksgiving. Check out all the juiciest moments we can't stop thinking about.

There's certainly a high chance you've heard a family member make that infamous request once everyone has gathered around the table for Thanksgiving, a time filled with aforementioned turkey and stuffing yourself with the requisite mashed potatoes, pumpkin pie and a whole lot of awkward small talk with those distant family members you see about as often as you go to the dentist.

"I know, I can't believe it's been so long." "Yes, I'm still single." "No, I haven't watched The Studio yet."

And that's why you need comfort food. No, we're not talking about Aunt Maureen's green bean casserole and the rest of the feast you're impatiently waiting to dive into, we're talking about comfort food for your soul that only a treasured TV show or movie can provide.

So if you're looking for a cozy distraction right now, we've rounded up some of our favorite Thanksgiving-themed episodes of shows like Gossip Girl, How I Met Your Mother and Friends (could the NBC series be any better at celebrating the football-and feast-focused holiday), as well as a few movies about Turkey Day.

Yes, there are actually plenty of films made about the Jan Brady of holidays, even if Halloween and Christmas tend to gobble up the majority of the attention at the end of each year.

Some are more showy about it (see: Planes, Trains & Automobiles) while others just make a passing reference, but thanks to that scene in Zabar's (featuring a pre-Grey's Anatomy Sara Ramirez) we want You've Got Mail to be a Thanksgiving movie, we want it so badly.

So, stockpile a plate of leftovers, hibernate in the basement and get ready to stream your long weekend away.

The iconic NBC sitcom is infamous for its annual Thanksgiving episodes, delivering 10 near-perfect holiday installments in its decade-long run. It's hard to pick just one (and we've done the ranking to prove it), so we're going to suggest three.

Season five's classic "The One With All the Thanksgivings" is notable for the delightful flashbacks and the first "I love you" between Chandler and Monica (who is wearing a turkey on her head, natch).

We suggest following that up with season six's "The One Where Ross Got High" because it's the group's dynamic at its very best, while season eight's "The One With the Rumor" is, of course, the one where Brad Pitt makes his iconic guest appearance as the co-founder of their high school's "I Hate Rachel Club." (Listen, if he can attend ex Jennifer Aniston's 50th birthday bash post-divorce and they can call each other "hun," we can highlight his ep!) (Where to watch: HBO Max)

Another sitcom about a close-knit group of friends with a penchant for nailing Thanksgiving episodes, fans could always count on HIMYM to deliver the goods. But the best outing is season three's iconic "Slapsgiving," which gave us the third (and arguably best) slap in Marshall and Barney's ongoing bet. Gather around the piano and sing it with us: "Ya just got slapped"! (Where to watch: Hulu, Disney+)

What better way to nurse your food coma than by watching Lorelai and Rory go on a Thanksgiving dinner-crawl, hitting four feasts in one day in season three's "A Deep-Fried Korean Thanksgiving"? Oy with the leftovers! (Where to watch: Netflix)

Two words: Pilgrim Rick! Leave it to the NBC series to hit us right in the feels, especially on Thanksgiving. In this season one episode, we see the origin of the Pearson family's Pilgrim Rick hat, with a flashback revealing the family's holiday unexpectedly spent in a roadside motel. It all ties beautifully together with the present, as we see the Big Three still struggling with the loss of Jack.

Of course, it can't always be warm and fuzzies, as Randall ("Thanksgiving dad is a hot dad!") learns a shocking secret Rebecca had been keeping from him his entire life. C'mon, what's Thanksgiving without a family scandal being unearthed? (Where to watch: Hulu)

Another show that loved to make an annual event out of Turkey Day was Gossip Girl, beginning with "Blair Waldorf Must Pie!" The season one standout gave us flashbacks of old Serena, the moment she and Dan realized they could've been siblings, and, most importantly, insight into Blair's struggle with an eating disorder.

Season two's serving is skippable, but season three's offering, "The Treasure of Serena Madre," is a fun one thanks to a classic awkward family dinner from hell when Serena has to pass the butter to Maureen a.k.a. the wife of the man she's hooking up with. (Oh hey, Aaron Tveit as creepy congressman Trip!) Leave it to S to always ruin Thanksgiving. (Where to watch: HBO Max)

C'mon, how could we not include "Bangsiving" on our list, the classic episode in which Schmidt forced the loft gang to each bring a date they thought would be compatible for someone else to their holiday dinner? (Where to Watch: Hulu)

Season two's "Thanks For the Memories" will have you feeling super nostalgic as it centers on the ABC hit's OG interns. George (RIP!) is forced to go turkey hunting, Izzie (somewhere far, far away!) tries to throw the ultimate holiday dinner and Meredith, Cristina (miss you every day!) and Alex (How dare you, sir?) hide out at the hospital. And if that's not enough nostalgia, there's some deliciously torturous Mer-Der drama and that Fall Out Boy song thrown in for good measure. Oh, the 2005 memories. (Where to Watch: Hulu, Disney+)

"It's a sham, but it's a sham with yams. A yam sham."

If you're only going to do one big Thanksgiving episode, you might as well do it right, like BtVS' season four holiday-themed outing, "Pangs." Desperate to give the Scooby gang the perfect Thanksgiving, Buffy goes full-Pilgrimzilla, Slayer duties (and lack of cooking skills) be damned. Alas, everything goes awry when Xander releases a vengeful Native American spirit, resulting in Spike becoming a vampire dart board. Oh, and there's a doozy of a mic drop reveal in the final moment. (Where to watch: Hulu)

Chrismukkah gets all the attention when it comes to the teen drama, but the Orange County crew knew how to do Thanksgiving, too.

In season one's holiday outing, "The Homecoming," Ryan has to return to Chino to help his imprisoned older brother with Marissa in tow. Unfortunately, for many fans, this trip introduced Theresa, she who would go on to break up the couple.

And who doesn't love some love triangle action in between dinner and dessert, which is exactly what Seth was getting into when he invited both Summer and Anna to the house and attempted to keep them from seeing other. Bad plan, Cohen. (Where to Watch: HBO Max)

For a more poignant take on the holiday episode, look no further than this Emmy Award-winning outing, which focused on Denise, Dev's BFF. The show relied on flashbacks to her Thanksgiving experiences past to show Lena Waithe's character slowly coming to terms with her sexuality and her relationship with her family. (Where to watch: Netflix)

The cozy and crisp autumnal vibes of Nora Ephron's swoonworthy version of the Upper East Side should be enough to earn the rom-com a spot on this list. But fun fact: The scene in which Tom Hanks smugly helps Meg Ryan out at the Zabar's checkout line actually takes place on Thanksgiving Day! Remember Sara Ramirez's iconic delivery of "Happy Thanksgiving back"? (Where to Watch: Buy or rent on Apple TV+)

C'mon, it's the definitive movie in the limited Thanksgiving movie genre. And it's hilarious, with knockout performances by Steve Martin and John Candy still making us laugh over 30 years later. (Where to watch: Paramount+)

This underrated gem of a movie will make you wonder why the hell you hadn't heard of it as soon as the end credits roll. Starring Holly Hunter, Robert Downey Jr., Dylan McDermott and a young Claire Danes, the 1995 movie was Jodie Foster's second outing as a director and captures that odd catch-22 you can only understand once you've moved away from your family and return for the holidays, immediately falling back into your old familial patterns and behaviors. (Where to watch: Paramount+)

Wait, before you protest and say the 1993 dark comedy is a Halloween movie, hear us out. We're counting this one because of the play Wednesday and Pugsley Addams are forced to take part in at Camp Chippewa, which is about the first Thanksgiving. Yes, a summer camp is performing a play about Thanksgiving for some reason, but you do you, Gary and Becky Granger!

Playing Pocahontas, Wednesday decides to rewrite the tale to bloody and vengefully hilarious results. Plus, there's also the so-f--ked-up-it's-funny "Turkey Day" song, with Pugsley, dressed as turkey, singing, "Eat us 'cause we're good and dead!" (Where to watch: Paramount+)

So long, Joey Potter! Katie Holmes earned rave reviews for her turn in this 2003 indie movie about a girl who invites her small town family to her apartment in NYC's Lower East Side apartment. As you can imagine, s--t gets messy. Patricia Clarkson delivers a stellar performance as April's mom, which earned her an Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actress. Also, remember "The Thong Song"? Yeah, Sisqo is in this movie, too. So that happens! (Where to watch: Tubi)

Thank you Freeform for answering our prayers and delivering an adorable rom-com-gone-sort-of-wrong. And bonus points for the setting, which has a college freshman (charmingly played by Olivia Holt) returning home for the first time. It's a situation ripe for drama, especially when we learned that a "turkey drop" is when your high school sweetheart dumps you during Thanksgiving break. Enter: Her brother's hot BFF. Okay, so technically this rom-com starring Emma Roberts and Luke Bracey covers almost every holiday ever created as the leads agree to be each other's platonic plus-ones for a whole calendar year, but two points. 1. It does feature Thanksgiving and 2. It is funny as f--k. (Where to Watch: Netflix)

What happens when you bring four families with their own traditions and backgrounds—Vietnamese, Latino, Jewish, and African American—together under one roof? All-caps DRAMA but multiplied by four. Kyra Sedgwick and Julianna Margulies star in this 2000 film. (Where to watch: Prime Video)

#746. Frozen Cast's $60 Million Salaries & More Secrets We Can't Let Go

Kristen Bell’s love for Frozen is an open door, but she’s not earning $60 million for the sequels. Brush the snow off your boots and find out more secrets from the Disney movie, turning 13 on Nov. 27.

The paycheck never bothered Kristen Bell anyway.

Still, the Frozen star was, well frozen in place after reading a report suggesting she and costars Idina Menzel, Jonathan Groff and Josh Gad were earning a whopping $60 million for their work on the sequels to the 2013 Disney hit.

“I think there’s been a lot misreported about that Frozen deal,” Bell stressed to Entertainment Tonight at the 2026 Actor Awards in March. “No, no, no, no, no that’s somebody making a lot of things up.”

Rumors aside, spending the last 13 years—and counting—as Princess Anna has been the gift that keeps on giving.

“But that said, am I happy to have that job and does it pay very well because it’s a successful franchise? Yes,” the Good Place alum added. “And I’m so grateful for it and I will continue to do it for the rest of my life if they’ll have me.”

Bell and the rest of the Frozen cast have certainly received a stamp of approval from fans. Since the film's November 27, 2013, debut, Frozen has solidified its place as a modern animated classic. (Grossing $1.31 billion and kicking off a whole icy new franchise doesn’t hurt either.)

But though the adventures of sisters Anna and Elsa (Menzel) as well as Kristoff (Groff) and snowman Olaf (Gad) continue on in 2019’s Frozen 2 and the forthcoming Frozen 3—a fourth film is also on the way—there was a blizzard of ideas to shovel through before filmmakers found the magic.

Case in point: in the earliest version in 2008 saw not only gave Elsa a different origin story as a jilted bride who wished to never feel pain again. “The wish froze her heart, so she would never feel pain—but she also couldn’t feel love again,” co-director Chris Buck revealed to Vanity Fair in 2023. “She couldn’t feel anything. She was basically a villain.”

As for Anna—their sisterhood also came later. In the beginning, he continued, “Anna and Elsa, they knew each other. They lived in the same village. Believing that Elsa was not a bad person, and was not evil, Anna was the one that was going to save Elsa.”

But ultimately, the creative team realized they had to let it go for a bit before bringing it back. But though, like the best movies before it, Frozen proved to be a bit of a fixer upper that now holds a special place in fans’ hearts.

If you want to find out more secrets about the beloved movie, keep reading…

1. An adaptation of Hans Christian Andersen's 1845 fairy tale The Snow Queen, Frozen was actually in development at Disney for almost a decade (and was briefly considered for a hand-drawn animated feature back in 1937).

The first modern attempt happened in 2002, and when 2003 also proved unsuccessful, more stalled attempts followed over the years. Frozen really didn't start coming together until Christopher Buck, who directed Tarzan, came aboard in 2008, but the film wasn't commissioned until 2011 following Tangled's box office success.

And in 2012, Jennifer Lee, who initially came on as a screenwriter, was named co-director, making her the first woman to direct an animated film by Walt Disney Animation Studios.

2. The movie was going to be titled The Snow Queen after the original fairy tale, but the filmmakers decided to change it to Frozen "because, to us, it represents the movie. Frozen plays on the level of ice and snow but also the frozen relationship, the frozen heart that has to be thawed," producer Peter Del Vecho explained to Bleeding Cool, denying it was inspired by Tangled. (The Snow Queen title was still used overseas.)

3. Idina Menzel and Kristen Bell auditioned and met with the producers of Tangled for the role of Rapunzel, which ultimately went to Mandy Moore. (Santino Fontana, who gave life to Anna's temporary fiancé Hans, originally auditioned for the role of Flynn in the 2010 film as well).

Bell, whose dream since she was a little girl was to voice a Disney character, was the "very first actress" to audition for Anna, with Lee saying, "We did audition a lot of people for that but she was the first and the best. We just fell in love with her."

4. Menzel's audition for Elsa, meanwhile, was actually a table-read with Bell before both had been officially cast, according to Lee.

"They read the whole script and at the end—we didn't have any songs written yet—and what they did was sing a duet and they sung 'Wind Beneath My Wings,' but they sung it like sisters and what you mean to me," she explained. "And there wasn't a dry eye in the house after they sang...that is when they knew, that was the whole potential and understanding the power of music and of what this emotional story can be."

5. In the early versions of the project, Elsa was actually the villain of the story (with one of the early concept art designs being inspired by Bette Midler and her "showgirl stage presence"), according to former Disney animation designer Claire Keane, who released the image on her web site.

"Originally, she was much more villainous," Buck allowed to Nerdist. "It's very easy to go in that direction for that type of character, but as the time went and we evolved the story, she became much more three-dimensional. Before, I thought she was one-dimensional but a very fully fleshed out character."

The moment the character really changed, though, was after they watched earlier cuts and realized it wasn't exactly working: "Someone came up with the brilliant idea...'what if the protagonist, Anna, and Elsa were related?'" art director Michael Giaimo revealed to Kidz World in 2014. "Because they weren't always siblings, they weren't always related, and that was the beginning of finding these characters."

6. The hardest character for the Frozen team to nail down aside from Elsa was actually Olaf, who was originally then-villainous Elsa's first guard.

"She created these snowman guards and Marshmallow was kind of a holdover from that because he was this scary snowman guard. Olaf was the very first guard she created," Buck explained, adding he was still funny at that time.

After changing the character of Elsa completely, it wasn't until the directors first sat down with Josh Gad that they found the character. "Josh adlibbed the line 'it's like a baby unicorn' and there was something about that innocence," Del Vecho told Kidz World.

7. One main character who wasn't originally in the movie was Hans, Anna's suitor-turned-villain, with Giaimo explaining, "Hans was never originally in the story in older versions...Kristoff always was in the story or a version of the Kristoff character and Anna. And then Hans was brought in at one point but he wasn't always a villain who turned initially, and then someone came up with the idea of him turning. He was always potentially a villain, but we gave it away much sooner."

8. Anna's oft-repeated "Wait what?" catchphrase? An ad-lib by Bell. She also slipped in one slightly off-color joke. "We slid it under the radar," she detailed to Vanity Fair of Anna's singing, "For years I've roamed these empty halls / Why have a ballroom with no balls?" The NSFW lyric almost got snipped, she admitted, "But then we were like, 'What are you talking about? That’s not what it means. Don’t be a perv.'"

11. After having a few of the first songs they originally composed for the film not make it in, songwriting couple Robert Lopez and Kristen Anderson-Lopez were feeling a little low, so they went for walk in Brooklyn's Prospect Park.

Listening to songs by Adele and Avril Lavigne and being surrounded by nature, Anderson-Lopez told Playbill, "We were in this kind of emo place of imagining what it would be like to be this perfect person who messed up once, and was chased away from everything she has known and all the people she has been sacrificing for."

Within a day, they would write the film's most iconic song that would go on to sell over 10 million copies in 2014 and win the Oscar for Best Original Song. All together now, "Let it go, let it goooooooo."

12. And after hearing "Let It Go" for the first time, Lee said she knew they had to rework the character of Elsa and her motivations completely.

"Half of us were crying. And then I just went, 'I have to rewrite the whole movie,'" she said on the Scriptnotes podcast. "I really, it was—I was just like I'm going to go lie down for a couple minutes. But it was the best thing. We knew we had the movie."

13. On the same podcast, Lee admitted there was "a lot of push and pull" when it came to Elsa's look after her transformation via "Let It Go" and how sexy to make her after this awakening.

"Everyone was seduced by her. And so there was this tug of war I think, a bit, of letting people have a little—people who wanted to have that a little and not be afraid of it, but not make it a sexual statement," the co-director explained. "It's more a moment of, for me, it was like you strut and you say nobody is looking, this is what I'm going to—I'm not going to be afraid of my sexuality. I'm not going to be afraid of who I am. I'm not going to be afraid of anything about myself."

14. After eagle-eyed fans spotted one of many easter eggs in the film—Tangled's Rapunzel (post haircut) and Eugene briefly appearing in a scene during the morning of Elsa's coronation—a compelling fan theory that tied together Frozen, Tangled and Little Mermaid surfaced: Anna and Elsa's parents died when their boat sank...what if it was when they were on their way to the Tangled pair's wedding? And what if the sunken ship in The Little Mermaid is the ship they were sailing on?!

15. This theory only works if you believe Anna and Elsa's parents actually did die in the shipwreck, something Buck speculated about in a Reddit AMA, saying, in his mind, the King and Queen of Arendelle, as well as their "baby boy," did not actually die after being shipwrecked. (Who knew they had a son?)

He said they washed up on the shore of a jungle and built "a tree house" before being "eaten by a leopard." That baby boy? Tarzan, of course.

"That's my fun little world," he later told MTV. While the theory isn't official (and definitely takes a hit when you factor in the events of Frozen II), Buck said, "Whatever people want to believe, go for it. If you want to tie them all together, then do it."

16. The original ending of the film was drastically different, with the earlier versions, of course, presenting Elsa as the villain and not having Anna and Elsa related.

Beginning with a prophecy about "a ruler with a frozen heart will bring destruction to the kingdom of Arendelle," viewers would learn Elsa became the Snow Queen after she was left at the altar and decided to freeze her own heart.

By the end of the film, Anna convinces Elsa to use her powers to save Arendelle from an avalanche started by Hans, with the ultimate reveal being the prophecy was actually about the two-faced prince. (Elsa's heart would then unfreeze, making her capable of love again.)

"The problem was that we felt like we had seen it before," Del Vecho told Entertainment Weekly of the original ending. "It wasn't satisfying. We had no emotional connection to Elsa—we didn't care about her because she had spent the whole movie being the villain. We weren't drawn in. The characters weren't relatable."

17. Despite reports suggestign the cast was set to rake in a jaw-dropping $60 million for more sequels, Bell made it clear that couldn't be further from the truth. "I think there's been a lot misreported about that Frozen deal, she told Entertainment Tonight at the 2026 Actor Awards. "No, no, no, no, that's somebody making a lot of things up."

She continued, "But that said, am I happy to have that job and does it pay very well because it's a successful franchise? Yes. And I'm so grateful for it and I will continue to do it for the rest of my life if they'll have me."

#745. Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?

From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.

"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.

"It feels like your eyes are burning," said Disha Ravi, co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven."

Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.

"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.

"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.

The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.

Failure to cut emissions quickly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today."

He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.

Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.

But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.

One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to a recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.

A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.

So far, a small but growing number of countries, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system."

France is sticking to a previously announced deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan."

Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.

It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.

And it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.

Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.

"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she said. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess."

#743. Scratchy Ireland still prove too strong for Australia at Twickenham

Tries: Henshaw (26), Timoney (37), Baloucoune (43), McNabney (73,81) Conversions: Prendergast (27,39,44,74,81) Penalties: Prendergast (43)

Tries: Williams (22), Thomas (56) Conversions: Gordon (23,57)

Ireland vs Australia Nations Championship 8:10pm Friday 27th November

Ireland rounded off their Nations Championship campaign with a sixth victory from seven Tests, defeating Australia 38-14 at Allianz Stadium Twickenham.

Such a record can only be matched by England and France, should either or both defeat New Zealand and South Africa this weekend, respectively - Ireland finished behind England on points difference and France due to bonus points in the northern hemisphere standings.

On Friday, centre Robbie Henshaw, back-row Nick Timoney, wing Rob Baloucoune and replacement No 8 James McNabney (two) scored tries, with Sam Prendergast adding all five conversions and a penalty.

Ireland - Tries: Henshaw (26), Timoney (37), Baloucoune (43), McNabney (73,80+1). Cons: Prendergast (26,39,44,74,80+1). Pens: Prendergast (40+3).

Australia - Tries: Williams (22), Thomas (56). Cons: Gordon (23, 57).

Andy Farrell's Ireland were far from their best on the night, but the Wallabies could only score two tries through lock Jeremy Williams and scrum-half Kalani Thomas, wasting a further nine 22 entries up against an extremely tough Irish defence.

The victory also saw Ireland claim the Raeburn Shield from Australia - rugby's lineal world title which dates back to the first Test match ever played in 1871. Australia had won it by beating Wales, who claimed it from New Zealand in Cardiff a fortnight ago.

Ireland began the contest well off the standard they produced in victory over world No 1-ranked South Africa last week, with their attack struggling to click and errors widespread.

Australia, despite a wealth of early possession and territory, produced a number of mistakes themselves, though, with fly-half Carter Gordon guilty of missing touch with a penalty from hand in the most glaring example.

In the end, it took until the 22nd minute for the Wallabies to strike for the opener: Williams scoring from close range after Tadhg Beirne had actually stolen an Australia five-metre lineout, but Ronan Kelleher had spilled to surrender possession back.

Within four minutes, Ireland were level, as they struck for a try off their very first 22 entry: a clever lineout move to the tail setting scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park breaking back down the blindside, before Kelleher was stopped just short.

Centre Stuart McCloskey did the damage from there, as he took on the ball and fed midfield partner Henshaw, who slid over untouched.

Three minutes from the end of the half, Ireland displayed their clinical nature again as Timoney scored following a well-constructed rolling maul to move Farrell's side in front.

Ireland almost had a third try before the break in the final play, only for centre Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii to stick out a hand in a deliberate knock-on. The Wallaby avoided a yellow card, but Prendergast stretched the lead to 10 points off the tee.

Into the second half, Ireland started far brighter, with Jacob Stockdale almost scoring down the left less than two minutes in, and Baloucoune then scoring a minute later after collecting a Prendergast cross-field kick James Ramm could only deflect into his path.

Prendergast converted for a 24-7 lead, and what ensued was virtually 10 minutes of sustained Australia attack in the Irish 22 for no points.

The Wallabies did finally cross for their second try through Thomas in the 55th minute, with the score surviving a TMO check into the grounding.

Gordon narrowed Ireland's lead to 10 points with the conversion, but they failed to build from there.

Instead, Ireland's pack tore forward for a scrum penalty against the head in the lead-up to their fourth try - impressive back-row McNabney showing his power off the bench to wrestle over by the posts.

In the final attack of the half, Ireland then blew out the scoreline beyond what had truly transpired in the contest, in truth, with the exciting McNabney finishing again.

Ireland head coach Andy Farrell told ITV Sport:

"Everyone could see it was a bit error-ridden with all sorts of things going on.

"But I suppose the way that we stayed composed and did it in our own way was a credit to how we kept on going.

"That was epitomised in the first half where we had no territory and no possession whatsoever, and we go in with the lead, which was very pleasing.

"It wasn't a brilliant performance, but at the same time I'm very pleased with the composure to make sure we keep on going.

"We would have taken that [going four from four] at the start, wouldn't we? Sport, when you're playing good sides in international rugby, doesn't always go your way.

"It didn't last week, but we still found a way. We did that today. We'll take that and we'll move on to the Six Nations.

"We're very pleased with the competition that we're building, and we've got a lot of good players back home who are dying to get back into the room.

Giving his verdict on Ireland's year, Brian O'Driscoll told ITV Sport:

"It was a disappointing Argentina, so you can't really gauge a huge amount. It was a good victory against them. Fiji, the expectation there is to win.

"The big one was South Africa, and they stood up to the plate there. They delivered a performance they should be proud of.

"This is a very well-settled team, except in one or two positions, and mainly your pivotal position at No 10.

"To give him [Prendergast] the confidence to guide the team around in a big game like that will go a long way towards restoring belief in all the players that have played 70, 80 Tests.

"But mostly for him as he's kind of forging his path as a relative newcomer to the Test Arena.

"I think, on the whole, very pleasing. If you had given us 10 victories in 12 games this calendar year, we'd have bitten your hand off, considering how they lost to France in the opening game of the Six Nations.

"The only other loss being to New Zealand in Eden Park.

"Are we World Cup contenders yet? I wouldn't say yes, no, I wouldn't. I think there's other teams a little bit ahead of us, but a year is a long way to go, and hopefully we can narrow that gap."

Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast told ITV:

"I think we stuck with it pretty well. There were some scrappy parts we'd like to be a bit better at.

"I thought we were quite clinical in their 22 but scrappy at times. I think he [Andy Farrell] will have a similar gist; there's definitely some good parts. There's loads we can be better at and want to be better at today.

"Coming into the autumn, we knew we had a couple of big games to start. We went four from four and that's what we were targeting. There was no lack of motivation.

"I'm really enjoying [playing for Ireland]. We're building towards the Rugby World Cup. Loads of highs and lows at the moment so, I won't get too high."

Australia head coach Les Kiss told ITV Sport:

"The first half we got some traction but we're disappointed with our end zone. Ireland were very clinical and took their chances when they came up.

"Credit to them, we needed to persist a bit longer. They were up for it. That was the difference; they took the key chances when they had to.

"Fair play to them, they put the scoreboard pressure on us. There's still a lot of good things there and a lot of things to look forward to, we've just got to build more consistency throughout our game."

Ireland are next in action during the 2027 Six Nations in February, when they start with a huge Test against England in Dublin at the Aviva Stadium on Friday February 5 (8.10pm kick-off).

Australia now enter their offseason and are not in action again until April 25 2027 when they face New Zealand at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane. Australia are hosting the Rugby World Cup in 2027 between October 1-November 13.

#742. Navigating grief in academia: ways to find balance

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Pamela Yeh is a professor of evolutionary biology at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Pamela Yeh with her mother in Los Angeles, California, in the late 1970s.Credit: Courtesy of Pamela Yeh

There are few things in this world that are more universal than grief. And yet, each person’s own particular grief can feel as unique as the person they are grieving for. I have been in academia for decades, but have heard little about grief in that time, so I wanted to share a few tips that helped me get through the early stages of grief when my mother died last year.

My mother grew up in deep poverty in Taiwan and she worked relentlessly throughout her life to give me and my siblings many opportunities. She was the first in her family to go to college, and at 23 years old, she moved to Canada to work as a nurse. After a few years of enduring Canadian winters, she had had enough and moved to sunny California. She met my dad there, and a few years later she gave birth to my sister, then me and then my brother. She raised us while working several jobs as a nurse. She cheered the three of us on throughout our lives. That’s not to say that she ever fully understood my career: she once described my work (I am an evolutionary biologist, specializing in birds and bacteria, at the University of California, Los Angeles) as “counting birds”.

She was adventurous, but between her family and work responsibilities, she didn’t have much time to travel. So, once she retired, I took her on fieldwork and conference trips with me whenever I could — to China, the Netherlands, Italy, Mexico, Japan and throughout the United States.

When her grandchildren came along, she helped them to learn how to read, to do maths and to speak Chinese. In the last years of her life, I had a small house built for her in our back garden in Los Angeles, so she would always be close to me. When you lose someone who is extremely close to you, your world is never the same.

When a loved one dies: how academia can support bereaved colleagues

When a loved one dies: how academia can support bereaved colleagues

In the weeks and months after she died, I found myself in a fog of shock and grief. I felt the need to be moving constantly: running, walking the dog, cleaning the house. At times, I could not be certain of my ability to conduct the high-level abstract and conceptual thinking that academia often requires, so I turned to Trevor Price, my former PhD adviser at the University of California, San Diego (who is now at the University of Chicago, Illinois). I explained my brain fog and deep grief, and he read over my work and made sure that I didn’t miss any crucial scientific arguments in some of the papers I was writing. Although I graduated more than two decades ago, he did not hesitate for one second to help me.

People won’t know that you need help until you reach out. And the earlier you do it, the more time and energy you can give yourself and the easier it will be for others to help.

Here are some tips that helped me to navigate the academic world while grieving.

Ideally, you should determine what support is available before it is needed. Institutions often have all sorts of resources and benefits for people experiencing grief. These might include time off for a bereavement, leave for family care, counselling and a break from teaching classes. I never knew, until my mother passed away, that I could have taken paid leave to take care of her while she was unwell: she had a debilitating stroke five months before she died. Make sure you understand (and ask questions) about your work contract and what your employer offers.

Sometimes, a family member’s illness can occur suddenly, and other times it might start off as one condition and snowball into something else. Talk to the chair of your department and to your colleagues as early as possible about getting cover for your courses and committees. Be creative and brainstorm which other people — including your colleagues, former advisers and former students and postdocs — might be able to step in and give your conference talks, guest lecture for your classes and conduct other activities that you might need help with.

Pamela Yeh (centre) with her parents, husband, son and dog on the front steps of her home in Los Angeles, California, in 2014.Credit: Courtesy of Pamela Yeh

I learnt this the hard way. I did not reach out to people early enough and was unrealistically optimistic about my mother’s health trajectory. While I waited for her to get better, I was so panicked about the thought of losing her that I became incapacitated. I couldn’t focus and, at times, I could barely do simple tasks such as answering e-mails, or making appointments for meetings. I told myself as soon as she was better, which would be any day now, I would catch up. And so, I didn’t have a realistic plan in place when she died.

You have to accept that you might not be at your best when it comes to research productivity, mentoring and teaching while you’re grieving. Ask someone to help with advising your students, and rely on colleagues or former students. You might have to reduce the frequency with which you meet your students, hold laboratory meetings and work with collaborators, and resort to advising through e-mail and video calls. And you might have to give less detailed comments on your students’ writing. I did all of the above during the first few weeks and months of grieving. I had an especially hard time giving advice to my graduate students who were doing field work. Ellie Diamant, a former PhD student of mine who is now a biologist at Bard College in Annandale-On-Hudson, New York, generously stepped in and met with many of my students. It took me a while to understand and accept that I simply wasn’t going to meet the normal standards I set for myself while going through this difficult time.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-02752-6
